claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi specimens have an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi specimens undergo a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
This transition produces a large magnetocaloric entropy change with substantial hysteresis.
Narrowly controlled rapid thermal annealing can introduce nanoscale strain heterogeneity and modify grain-boundary characteristics in as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi.
The annealing treatment can modify defects without causing microstructural coarsening or changing the overall hexagonal phase.
Annealing-induced strain heterogeneity and engineered grain boundaries lower local energy barriers for phase-boundary motion.
Lower phase-boundary barriers make the magnetostructural transformation smoother and more reversible.
Annealing will broaden the transition and produce a slightly wider magnetic-entropy-change peak.
Annealed samples will have lower hysteresis-loop area or coercive-field offsets than the as-deposited control.
The annealed samples will retain a substantial magnetocaloric entropy change.
The specimens' maintained high surface-to-volume ratio will improve their heat-exchange rate after annealing.
Deposition-induced microstructural features in the baseline specimens impede smooth phase-boundary movement and cause large hysteretic losses.
The predicted benefit exists only within an annealing window that avoids deleterious grain growth and phase changes.
The response should be reproducible in similarly deposited specimens during low-field cycling near the intrinsic transition temperature.
The relevant FeMnNiGeSi magnetostructural transition occurs around ambient temperature.
The magnitude of hysteresis reduction and entropy-change retention depends sensitively on annealing temperature, duration, cooling rate, and initial defect density.

contradictions.description: The as-deposited thin-film baseline is described as having limited heat-exchange performance, but the annealed specimen's improved heat exchange is attributed to maintaining the same high surface-to-volume ratio. Because the intervention does not change that ratio, it cannot by itself explain a relative heat-exchange improvement.
